claim: A receiver needs at least four pseudo-ranges: three for its position and one for its clock. The geometry of the satellites (the DOP) sets how range errors grow into position errors.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §3.1
ai_rationale: Four unknowns (three coordinates and the receiver clock offset) need at least four pseudo-ranges, and the DOP turns range errors into position errors; the receiver code gives no fix with fewer than four satellites. Textbook GNSS, checked from expertise: Doc 9849 §3.1 itself was not read.

claim: The GPS nominal constellation: 24 satellites in six orbital planes, about 20 200 km high, inclined 55°, one orbit in about 12 hours.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §3.2.2; US Department of Defense SPS PS §3.2, Tables 3.2-1 and 3.2-3
ai_rationale: The GPS SPS Performance Standard (read) gives 24 baseline slots in six planes, 55° inclination and a 26 559.8 km semi-major axis, about 20 180 km above the equator, with an orbit of half a sidereal day. The model’s 20 200 km gives 11.98 h instead of 11.97 h, negligible for teaching; the SPS PS is now cited.

claim: The model spaces the 24 satellites evenly (a Walker 24/6/1 pattern); the real slots are not evenly spaced.
sources: US Department of Defense SPS PS §3.2, Table 3.2-1
note: A simplification the page keeps; it changes the geometry, not the principles.
ai_rationale: The text is right: the SPS PS slot table (read) has uneven arguments of latitude in each plane (plane A: 13.22°, 133.20°, 239.54°, 343.09°), and the model’s even Walker 24/6/1 pattern is a labelled simplification. The source was wrong: IS-GPS-200 defines the signal, not the slots, so the claim now cites the SPS PS. Both reviewers agree.

claim: The model flies the nominal 24 satellites; the operational GPS constellation has more (about 31 in recent years). With GPS alone, gaps in RAIM coverage are therefore more frequent in the model than in reality, so each scenario starts its constellation where its approach has typical geometry: RAIM supports LNAV, as it does on almost every real approach.
note: Modelling the operational constellation would be more faithful; it would change the recorded AirNav Indonesia results (tests/golden).
ai_rationale: gps.gov (read) gave 31 operational satellites in July 2023 against a commitment of at least 24, so "about 31" holds. Flying the nominal 24 makes RAIM gaps more frequent, and starting each scenario at a typical geometry is an honest, labelled modelling choice. Doc 9849 §4.3.4.3 was not read.

claim: The model lets every GPS satellite broadcast L5; not every GPS satellite does today.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §3.2.4
note: GPS L5 is broadcast only by Block IIF and later satellites (IS-GPS-200N §6.2.5) and is not yet declared operational for safety-of-life use; confirm its status on gps.gov before a presentation.
ai_rationale: IS-GPS-200N §6.2.5 (read) says only Block IIF and later satellites broadcast L5; the claim says the model simplifies that. GPS L5 is also not yet declared operational for safety-of-life use, which the note now says; its status should be checked on gps.gov before a presentation.

claim: GPS civil signals: L1 at 1575.42 MHz and L5 at 1176.45 MHz; all GPS satellites share each frequency (CDMA).
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §3.2.4
ai_rationale: IS-GPS-200N (read) gives L1 at 1575.42 MHz (§3.3.1.1) and L5 at 1176.45 MHz (§6.2.5; the L5 signal itself is in IS-GPS-705); all GPS satellites share the carriers (CDMA). The code holds exactly these values.

claim: The speed of light is 299 792 458 m/s (exact, by definition of the metre).
sources: US Space Force IS-GPS-200
ai_rationale: IS-GPS-200N (read) uses c = 2.99792458 × 10⁸ m/s in its user algorithms; the value is exact because the SI metre is defined from it. The code matches.

claim: WGS-84: semi-major axis 6 378 137.0 m, flattening 1/298.257223563.
sources: NIMA (now NGA) TR8350.2
ai_rationale: a = 6 378 137.0 m and 1/f = 298.257223563 are two of the four WGS-84 defining parameters. Confirmed through search results quoting NGA and the ICG WGS 84 summary, not from TR8350.2 itself; the values are well established and the code matches to 1e-12.

claim: The Earth rotates at 7.292115 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s (WGS-84), the value the model uses. GPS receivers use the IS-GPS-200 value, 7.2921151467 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, when they compute positions from the broadcast ephemeris; for the model’s idealised orbits the difference is negligible (less than a millimetre).
sources: NIMA (now NGA) TR8350.2; US Space Force IS-GPS-200
ai_rationale: WGS-84 defines ω = 7 292 115 × 10⁻¹¹ rad/s, and IS-GPS-200N Table 20-IV (read) gives 7.2921151467 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s for the GPS user equations. The IS-GPS value is needed only when computing positions from the broadcast ephemeris; on the model’s idealised orbits the difference is below a millimetre, so the open question in the text is closed.

claim: The Earth’s gravitational constant used for GPS orbits: 3.986005 × 10¹⁴ m³/s².
sources: US Space Force IS-GPS-200
ai_rationale: IS-GPS-200N Table 20-IV (read) gives μ = 3.986005 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² as the WGS 84 value for GPS users. The current WGS-84 GM is 3.986004418 × 10¹⁴, but GPS deliberately keeps the older value, so "used for GPS orbits" is the right wording.

claim: A range is wrong because of the satellite clock, the orbit, the ionosphere (usually the largest), the troposphere, multipath and receiver noise. SBAS corrects the first three for its region; the receiver models the troposphere; multipath and noise stay.
ai_rationale: These are the standard range-error sources, the ionosphere usually the largest on L1. SBAS corrects clock, orbit and (on its grid) the ionosphere, the receiver models the troposphere, and multipath and noise enter only its error bound. Checked from expertise; Doc 9849 §4.3.1.1 and §5.2.1 were not read.

claim: Illustrative 1σ sizes of the GPS broadcast clock (1.1 m) and orbit (0.8 m) errors along the line of sight.
sources: US Department of Defense SPS PS §3.4.1, Table 3.4-1
note: The truth is drawn at about 0.95 m 1σ (about 1.9 m 95 %), consistent with the SPS PS commitment of 2.0 m 95 % global average URE for the ensemble of constellation slots (7.0 m 95 % per satellite); the split between clock and orbit is illustrative.
ai_rationale: As illustrative values they are acceptable: the truth is drawn at about 0.95 m 1σ (about 1.9 m 95 %), consistent with the SPS PS commitment of 2.0 m 95 % for the ensemble of constellation slots (Table 3.4-1 also gives 7.0 m 95 % per satellite). IS-GPS-200 has no error budget, so the claim now cites the SPS PS; the second reviewer sharpened which SPS PS figure applies.

claim: The receiver’s tropospheric model: mapping m(E) = 1.001 / √(0.002001 + sin²E), residual σ of 0.12 m at the zenith.
sources: RTCA DO-229 Appendix A
ai_rationale: The mapping 1.001/√(0.002001 + sin²E) and the 0.12 m zenith residual σ are the RTCA MOPS tropospheric model (Navipedia, read, confirms the mapping; search results the 0.12 m). The MOPS adds a small term below 4° elevation, irrelevant at the 5° mask. DO-229 was not read, so a reviewer with it should sign off.

claim: Airborne multipath σ = 0.13 + 0.53·e^(−θ/10°) m (the standard airframe multipath model) and receiver noise σ = 0.36 m, the largest the SBAS receiver may have for a GPS signal at minimum received power (0.15 m at maximum power).
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B 3.5.8.4.1 (receiver noise), 3.6.5.5.1.1.2 (multipath, referenced for SBAS by the Note to 3.5.8.4.2); Attachment D 6.3.9; RTCA DO-229
ai_rationale: The multipath model 0.13 + 0.53·e^(−θ/10°) m is the standard airframe model (Annex 10 App B 3.6.5.5.1.1.2, applied to SBAS by the Note to 3.5.8.4.2), and 0.36 m is the receiver-noise limit at minimum signal power, 0.15 m at maximum (App B 3.5.8.4.1); the second reviewer read both. The "AAD-A-like" label was replaced: Att D 6.3.9 does use GBAS AAD-A for SBAS service prediction, but AAD-A varies with elevation while the code’s 0.36 m is the constant SBAS limit.

claim: Reference stations at surveyed positions over a large area monitor the satellites and send their data to master stations.
ai_rationale: The standard description of the SBAS ground segment: reference stations (RIMS in EGNOS) at surveyed positions over a wide area monitor the GNSS signals and send their measurements to the master stations. The EGNOS SoL SDD (read) describes its RIMS network the same way.

claim: Master stations compute clock and orbit corrections for each satellite and ionospheric delays on a grid, and bound what is left.
ai_rationale: Master stations compute satellite clock and orbit corrections, vertical ionospheric delays at the grid points, and integrity bounds on what is left (UDRE, GIVE), as the SARPs describe and Walter’s WAAS MOPS examples (read) show.

claim: UDRE bounds the residual clock and orbit error of each satellite; GIVE bounds the error of each grid point’s ionospheric delay.
ai_rationale: UDRE (via UDREI) bounds each satellite’s residual clock and orbit error at 99.9 %, GIVE (via GIVEI) the residual vertical ionospheric error at each grid point; the receiver turns both into variances for its protection levels, as RTKLIB’s DO-229 implementation (read) does.

claim: "Do Not Use" (UDREI 15) and "Not Monitored" (UDREI 14) satellites cannot be used with SBAS integrity; for precision approach and APV (LNAV/VNAV, LPV) a satellite with UDREI 12 or 13 (UDRE 50 m or 150 m) cannot be used either.
value: 12, 14, 15 UDREI (first not usable for precision approach and APV, Not Monitored, Do Not Use)
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B 3.5.8.1.2.12; ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.1.3
note: Annex 10 states the rule for precision approach and APV; LP is left out until RTCA DO-229 is checked.
ai_rationale: Annex 10 App B 3.5.8.1.2.12 (read by the second reviewer) says the receiver shall no longer use a satellite for SBAS precision approach or APV if its UDREI is 12 or more; the claim and the code had allowed UDREI 12. The claim now says so and the receiver rule (groundSegment.usableForPa) refuses UDREI ≥ 12 for LNAV/VNAV and LPV. Doc 9849 §4.3.1.3 covers only Do Not Use and Not Monitored, so there is no conflict; LP is left out until DO-229 is checked.

claim: The UDREI table: UDRE 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 3.0, 3.75, 4.5, 5.25, 6.0, 7.5, 15, 50 and 150 m for UDREI 0–13; 14 is Not Monitored and 15 Do Not Use.
sources: RTCA DO-229 Table A-6; ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B
ai_rationale: The 14 UDRE values (0.75 to 150 m for UDREI 0–13; 14 Not Monitored, 15 Do Not Use) are the UDREI table; RTKLIB’s DO-229 variance table (read) is exactly (UDRE/3.29)² for these values. The DO-229 table number was not checked against the text.

claim: σ_UDRE is taken as UDRE / 3.29 (UDRE bounds 99.9 %); DO-229 tabulates σ²_UDRE for each UDREI, and the two agree to the table’s rounding (UDREI 0: 0.0520 m²).
sources: RTCA DO-229 Table A-6
ai_rationale: The tabulated σ²_UDRE at UDREI 0 is 0.0520 m² and (0.75/3.29)² = 0.05197 m²; the whole column equals (UDRE/3.29)² rounded up in the fourth decimal, 3.29 being the two-sided 99.9 % Gaussian factor.

sources: RTCA DO-229 Table A-17
ai_rationale: The 15 GIVE values (0.3 to 45 m for GIVEI 0–14; 15 Not Monitored) match the GIVEI table, and RTKLIB’s σ²_GIVE table (read) equals (GIVE/3.29)² for exactly these. The value array ends with the Not Monitored index 15, which the unit "m" does not make clear.

claim: σ_GIVE is taken as GIVE / 3.29; DO-229 tabulates σ²_GIVE for each GIVEI (GIVEI 0: 0.0084 m²).
sources: RTCA DO-229 Table A-17
ai_rationale: DO-229 tabulates σ²_GIVE = 0.0084 m² at GIVEI 0 (RTKLIB’s copy, read); GIVE/3.29 gives 0.00831 m², about 1 % lower because the standard rounds its variances up. The difference is inside the claim’s 2 % tolerance and does not matter for teaching.

claim: Ionospheric grid points are 5° apart in latitude and longitude between 55°S and 55°N.
sources: RTCA DO-229 IGP bands
ai_rationale: In IGP bands 0–8 the grid points are every 5° between 55°S and 55°N and wider poleward (RTKLIB’s band tables, read). Both scenarios’ grids lie inside 55°S–55°N, so a uniform 5° grid is right for them.

claim: The ionosphere is modelled as a thin shell 350 km above the Earth; pierce points and the obliquity factor follow from it.
sources: RTCA DO-229 Appendix A
ai_rationale: The SBAS user algorithm puts the pierce point on a thin shell 350 km above an Earth of radius 6378.1363 km and derives the obliquity from the same geometry; RTKLIB’s DO-229 implementation (read) uses exactly these constants.

claim: Uplink stations send the messages to the SBAS GEO satellites, which rebroadcast them; a GEO stays over the equator at a fixed longitude.
ai_rationale: Uplink stations (NLES in EGNOS) send the message stream to the GEOs, which rebroadcast it; a GEO stays over the equator at a nominally fixed longitude, drifting slightly inside its station-keeping box, which the page can ignore. The EGNOS SoL SDD (read) describes the space segment the same way.

claim: An SBAS GEO broadcasts one 250-bit message every second (250 bit/s, 500 symbols/s after forward error correction). On L1 a message is an 8-bit preamble, a 6-bit type, 212 data bits and a 24-bit CRC.
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B; RTCA DO-229
note: The recorded EGNOS messages (src/replay) confirm the L1 layout: every one passes the 24-bit CRC over this layout and starts with an 8-bit preamble.
ai_rationale: Each GEO sends one 250-bit message a second, rate-½ encoded to 500 symbols/s; an L1 message is an 8-bit share of the 24-bit preamble, a 6-bit type, 212 data bits and a 24-bit CRC. The Annex 10 App B text read gives the preamble and the data field, the symbol rate and FEC come from expertise, and the recorded EGNOS messages confirm the layout.

claim: A DFMC message on L5 is also 250 bits a second, but with a 4-bit preamble: 4 + 6 + 216 + 24 bits.
sources: EUROCAE ED-259; ICAO Annex 10 DFMC SBAS SARPs
note: The 4-bit preamble is confirmed by public summaries of the DFMC SARPs; 216 data bits follow from the 250-bit total.
ai_rationale: On L5 the 24-bit preamble is spread over six messages, so each carries 4 preamble bits, a 6-bit type, 216 data bits and a 24-bit CRC, 250 bits a second; the draft DFMC Annex 10 text (read) shows this. Type 50 (authentication) is the one exception, without a CRC, which does not matter here.

claim: The message type numbers and names (L1: 1 PRN mask, 2–5 fast corrections, 6 integrity, 7 fast-correction degradation, 9 GEO navigation, 10 degradation, 12 network time, 17 GEO almanac, 18 IGP mask, 24 mixed, 25 long-term, 26 ionospheric delays, 27/28, 63 null; DFMC: 31, 32, 34, 37, 39, 47).
sources: RTCA DO-229; EUROCAE ED-259; ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.4.2; ICAO Doc 9849 Appendix G 2.5; EUSPA SoL SDD §4.1.2 Table 4; FAA Global Positioning System Wide Area Augmentation System (… Table 2.1-1
note: Doc 9849 names Types 0, 27, 28 and 32. The L1 numbers and names agree with EGNOS SoL SDD v3.6 Table 4 and the WAAS PS Table 2.1-1; EGNOS broadcasts no Type 28, so the page’s L1 broadcast plan leaves it out. The recorded EGNOS broadcast (2011) contains Types 1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 10, 12, 17, 18, 24, 25, 26 and 27. The DFMC numbers (ED-259) are to confirm.
ai_rationale: All numbers and names match the Annex 10 tables of L1 and L5 message types (read in the draft amendment). Minor naming nits: Type 39 is "SBAS satellite clock, ephemeris and covariance matrix, part 1", and Type 37 also carries the DFREI scale table.

claim: Message Type 0 means "do not use this SBAS for safety-of-life"; Types 27 and 28 (L1) and 32 (DFMC) bound the errors away from the network.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 Appendix G 2.5; ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.4.2
ai_rationale: Type 0 means Do Not Use (test mode): the receiver drops that SBAS satellite’s data for at least a minute. Type 27 or 28 on L1 (a provider sends one or the other) and the covariance in Type 32 on L5 make the bound depend on the user’s position, as the claim says.

claim: How long received data may be used: the integrity data (UDREI) 12 s for precision approach and APV (LNAV/VNAV, LPV) and 18 s for en route, terminal and NPA; the fast corrections themselves time out after I_fc, set by the degradation factor in Message Type 7 (12 to 120 s for approach, 18 to 180 s otherwise); long-term corrections 240 s / 360 s; the ionospheric corrections 600 s. During an approach with HAL ≤ 40 m or VAL ≤ 50 m, losing 4 successive messages invalidates all UDREI data, so LPV and LNAV/VNAV end after 4 s without a GEO signal.
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B Table B-94, Table B-95, 3.5.8.1.2.7, 3.5.8.1.2.8; FAA William J. Hughes Technical Center WAAS Performance Analysis Report #92 (1 January to 31 Mar… Table 5-3; RTCA DO-229 Table A-25; EUROCAE ED-259
note: The GEO-loss behaviour uses the four-lost-messages rule for vertical guidance and the 18 s UDREI time-out for en route to NPA. LP is not named in the Annex 10 columns, so it is not put in the 12 s column until DO-229 is checked. The four-messages rule (App B 3.5.8.1.2.7) is to confirm in DO-229; the WAAS PAN report gives the same time-outs as Table B-94.
ai_rationale: Re-checked after the text added the four-lost-messages rule. Annex 10 App B Table B-94 (read in the 8th edition by the second reviewer) gives the integrity data (UDREI) 12 s for precision approach and APV and 18 s for en route, terminal and NPA, long-term corrections 240/360 s and Type 26 600 s; the fast corrections time out after I_fc from Type 7 (Table B-95); 3.5.8.1.2.7, read in the same pass, invalidates all UDREI data after four successive lost messages with HAL ≤ 40 m or VAL ≤ 50 m, which the GEO-loss behaviour now applies (it had kept LPV for the full 12 s). The WAAS PAN report #92 Table 5-3, read for this re-check, gives the same 12/18, 240/360 and 600 s.

claim: The page’s detection (2.5 s) and uplink (1.2 s) latencies are illustrative; the requirement is the time to alert.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 Table 2-1
ai_rationale: The 2.5 s detection and 1.2 s uplink latencies are not specified values, and the claim labels them so. In the code the aircraft gets the alarm at most about 5.7 s after the fault, within the 6 s time to alert of Category I and APV-II and the 10 s of APV-I, so the page does not mislead.

claim: With satellite status and clock and orbit corrections, SBAS supports departure to non-precision approach; with the ionospheric grid too, approaches with vertical guidance up to Category I.
ai_rationale: The SARPs define the SBAS functions as ranging, satellite status, basic differential correction (clock and orbit) and precise differential correction (adding the ionospheric grid); status and basic corrections support departure to NPA, precise corrections APV and Category I. Checked from expertise; the cited sections were not read.

claim: The receiver combines UDRE, GIVE and its own error models into protection levels (HPL, VPL) and compares them with the alert limits (HAL, VAL).
ai_rationale: The receiver combines σ_flt (from UDRE and degradation), σ_UIRE (from GIVE) and its own airborne and troposphere models into HPL and VPL, and the operation is available only while each stays within HAL and VAL: the standard SBAS integrity check, as Walter’s examples (read) show.

claim: HPL = K_H·d_major and VPL = K_V·d_V, with K_H = 6.0 for approaches with vertical guidance and 6.18 otherwise, and K_V = 5.33.
sources: RTCA DO-229 Appendix J; ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B
ai_rationale: K_H,NPA = 6.18, K_H,PA = 6.0 and K_V,PA = 5.33, with HPL = K_H·d_major and VPL = K_V·d_V, are the SBAS protection-level equations as known from DO-229 and Annex 10; Walter’s paper (read) plots the 5.33σ vertical bound. The exact paragraphs were not checked.

claim: GPS alone uses RAIM/FDE; its detection thresholds and protection-level factors are illustrative values (false-alarm probability about 10⁻⁵ per epoch, missed-detection probability 10⁻³).
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §4.2; RTCA DO-229 §2.1 FDE requirements
note: Recomputed in the AI check: the χ² thresholds (19.51 … 41.30) match Pfa 10⁻⁵; the earlier factors (5.4 … 7.2) gave a missed-detection probability of 0.08 to 0.16 and an HPL about 30 % too small. RTCA DO-229 states its false-alert requirement per hour, not per epoch (to confirm).
ai_rationale: Both reviewers recomputed independently: the χ² thresholds (19.51 … 41.30) match a false-alarm probability of 10⁻⁵ for 1–10 degrees of freedom, but the protection-level factors 5.4 … 7.2 gave a missed-detection probability of 0.08–0.16, not 10⁻³. The code now uses √λ for 10⁻³ (7.51 … 8.92), which raises the RAIM HPL by 24–39 %, and the text states both probabilities. DO-229’s false-alert requirement (per hour, not per epoch) was not read, so the per-epoch figure stays a labelled simplification.

claim: For SBAS approaches with vertical guidance, the avionics use only satellites at or above 5° elevation; the page applies the same 5° mask in every phase of flight and to the reference stations, as a simplification.
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B 3.5.8.1.2.11; EUSPA SoL SDD §6; RTCA DO-229
ai_rationale: Annex 10 App B 3.5.8.1.2.11 (read) says that for SBAS precision approach or APV the receiver uses only satellites at or above 5°; it sets no mask for en route or NPA, and none for reference stations. The claim said satellites below 5° are "not tracked" by aircraft and stations alike; it now cites the paragraph and labels the all-phases and RIMS mask as the page’s simplification. The EGNOS SoL SDD §6 (read) assumes the same 5°.

claim: GPS alone: the σ of the broadcast-model ionospheric residual is the larger of T_iono/5 and τ_vert times the obliquity, with τ_vert = 9 m where the pierce point is within 20° of the equator, 4.5 m from 20° to 55° and 6 m beyond (the model Annex 10 gives for an SBAS receiver that is not applying SBAS ionospheric corrections; the page also uses it for GPS alone).
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B 3.5.5.6.3.2; RTCA DO-229 Appendix J
note: The bands are on the geographic latitude of the pierce point (φ_pp), as Annex 10 defines them. The same σ serves L1 SBAS satellites outside the ionospheric grid and the service-area maps.
ai_rationale: Annex 10 App B 3.5.5.6.3.2 (read, page image checked) gives σ = max(T_iono/5, F_pp·τ_vert) with τ_vert 9 m within 20° of the equator, 4.5 m from 20° to 55° and 6 m beyond, on the geographic latitude of the pierce point (the first reviewer’s recollection of DO-229 said magnetic latitude). The code used 9 m everywhere, twice the standard value over Europe; one shared function (iono.sigmaIonoNoSbasM) now serves GPS alone, L1 SBAS satellites outside the grid and the service maps. Applying it to ABAS RAIM is a labelled modelling choice.

claim: The DFMC service’s correction bound (DFRE) is modelled with the same bound as UDRE; the DFREI table of ED-259 differs.
sources: EUROCAE ED-259
ai_rationale: DFMC SBAS bounds each satellite with DFRE (a DFREI in Types 32 and 34–36, scaled by the table in Type 37); the page reuses the L1 UDRE bound and says so. That changes only the size of the dual-frequency protection levels, not the idea, and is acceptable for teaching.

claim: The avionics annunciate the highest level of service the signal supports: LPV, LNAV/VNAV or LNAV.
ai_rationale: SBAS avionics annunciate the approach service level the signal currently supports (LPV, LNAV/VNAV, LNAV). The full list also has LP and advisory "+V" modes, but neither scenario has an LP procedure, so leaving them out does not mislead.

claim: The final approach segment (FAS) data block defines the LPV final approach, and a CRC protects it.
ai_rationale: The FAS data block defines the LPV/LP final approach path in the navigation database, and a 32-bit CRC inside it lets the avionics detect any corruption; the EUROCONTROL FAS tool (read) lists the CRC as part of the block.

claim: The FAS data block’s main fields (operation type, SBAS provider, airport, runway, approach performance designator, route indicator, reference path, landing threshold point, flight path alignment point, threshold crossing height, glide path angle, course width, HAL, VAL), with a typical 105 m course width at the threshold (80–143.75 m allowed).
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B Table B-96; RTCA DO-229 Appendix D; EUROCONTROL SBAS FAS Data Block Tool, source reference documentation
ai_rationale: Every field named is a real FAS field, but the list read as complete and left out the flight path alignment point, which with the threshold sets the final approach course. Annex 10 App B Table B-96 (read) lists the fields; the claim now names the main ones and the allowed course width, 80 to 143.75 m in 0.25 m steps (Doc 8168 Vol II’s worked example uses 105 m).

claim: The FAS data block CRC is a 32-bit CRC (CRC-32Q, polynomial 0x814141AB).
sources: RTCA DO-229
note: The CRC of the single byte 0x01 is the polynomial itself, which is how the binding reads it.
ai_rationale: The FAS data block CRC uses the 32-bit "Q" polynomial, 0x814141AB without the x³² term; the binding is valid because the CRC of the single byte 0x01 (MSB first, zero start) is the polynomial. The page computes it over a text encoding rather than the bit-packed block, an acknowledged simplification.

claim: Crews can select an SBAS approach by its five-digit channel number.
ai_rationale: Each SBAS approach has a five-digit channel number the crew can enter to select it, as with GBAS. Checked from expertise; Doc 9849 §4.3.2.9 was not read.

claim: SBAS approach channels run from 40 000 to 99 999.
sources: RTCA DO-229
ai_rationale: SBAS channels run from 40 000 to 99 999 (GBAS uses 20 001 to 39 999), and both scenario channels (54201, 40642) fall in the SBAS range. The paragraph number in Annex 10 or DO-229 was not checked.

claim: LPV deviations: lateral full scale is the course width at the threshold and widens at a constant angle measured from the azimuth reference point 305 m beyond the flight path alignment point (an ILS-like splay, about 1.5–2° for a typical runway); vertical full scale is a quarter of the glide path angle.
value: 305 m (azimuth reference point beyond the FPAP)
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B, FAS data block note; Attachment D 7.11.3.1–7.11.3.2, Figure D-15; RTCA DO-229
note: The page puts the flight path alignment point at the far end of the runway. Its ±1 NM limit on the lateral full scale is not in Annex 10 or Doc 8168 Vol II and is to be confirmed against RTCA DO-229; it never binds on the final approach shown.
ai_rationale: Annex 10 (read: the FAS data block note, Att D 7.11.3.1–7.11.3.2, Figure D-15) makes the lateral deviation angular about the azimuth reference point 305 m beyond the FPAP, with full scale equal to the course width at the threshold; the vertical full scale is 0.25 × the glide path angle. The code splayed linearly at about half that rate; it now widens the full scale as CW·(d + D)/D. The ±1 NM limit is in neither Annex 10 nor Doc 8168, so it stays in the code labelled to confirm against DO-229.

claim: The decision height of each scenario’s LPV procedure is illustrative: 250 ft at Bali, 200 ft for the LPV-200 at Nice.
ai_rationale: Each procedure sets its own decision height, and the page labels both values illustrative: 250 ft is typical of an APV-I LPV with VAL 50 m (Bali), and 200 ft needs the 35 m VAL of LPV-200 (Nice). Both match the scenarios’ alert limits.

claim: For LNAV/VNAV, LP and LPV the avionics must be able to track two SBAS satellites, so they can switch if one is lost; one satellite with current data is enough to fly the approach.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.2.10; ICAO Doc 9849 Appendix G §2.4.1; EUSPA SoL SDD §3.3.1
note: The model keeps LPV with one GEO and loses it when both are lost (after the time-out).
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §4.3.2.10 and Appendix G §2.4.1 (read) require the avionics to track the GEOs broadcasting corrections and to be able to switch quickly; the EGNOS SoL SDD §3.3.1 (read) says two operational GEOs secure a switching capability. As written, the claim read as if LPV were lost with one GEO; it now says one satellite with current data is enough, which is what the model does.

claim: Outside SBAS service, SBAS avionics fall back to ABAS (GPS alone with RAIM) automatically.
ai_rationale: When SBAS integrity is unavailable, SBAS avionics revert automatically to GPS with RAIM/FDE for en route to LNAV and lose the vertical SBAS modes, as DO-229 equipment does; the EGNOS SoL SDD (read) describes the same reversion.

claim: SBAS approaches need no dedicated equipment at the airport.
ai_rationale: An SBAS approach needs no navigation aid at the airport: the signal comes from the GEOs and the path from the FAS data block in the database. The airport still needs a surveyed, published procedure, but no dedicated equipment.

claim: A 35 m VAL supports a 200 ft decision height (LPV-200, equivalent to ILS Category I); in more than 1.76 billion WAAS observations with a VAL of 35 m or less, the largest signal-in-space vertical error was 8.9 m. Annex 10 requires a system-specific safety analysis before a VAL above 10 m is used.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.3.3; ICAO Annex 10 Chapter 3 Table 3.7.2.4-1 Note 2; Attachment D 3.3.6
note: The statistic is quoted from Doc 9849 (3rd edition, §4.3.3.3); its section number in the 5th edition is to confirm.
ai_rationale: The first reviewer could not trace the WAAS statistic; the second found it in Doc 9849 (3rd ed.) §4.3.3.3: in more than 1.76 billion observations with a VAL of 35 m or less, the largest WAAS signal-in-space vertical error was 8.9 m. Annex 10 Table 3.7.2.4-1 Note 2 (read) gives the Category I VAL as 35 to 10 m, a value above 10 m only after a system-specific safety analysis (Att D 3.3.6). The text now says what the statistic measured; its 5th-edition section number is to confirm.

claim: Alert limits and time to alert per operation: oceanic en route HAL 7.4 km, continental en route 3.7 km (5 min); terminal 1.85 km (15 s); NPA 556 m (10 s); APV-I HAL 40 m, VAL 50 m (10 s); APV-II 40 m / 20 m (6 s); Category I 40 m / 35–10 m (6 s; SBAS uses 35 m).
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 Table 2-1; ICAO Annex 10 Table 3.7.2.4-1
ai_rationale: Every value matches Annex 10 Vol I Table 3.7.2.4-1 and its Note 2 and Doc 9849 Table 2-1, both read: HAL 7.4 km, 3.7 km, 1.85 km, 556 m and 40 m, VAL 50 m, 20 m and 35–10 m, and the times to alert. "SBAS uses 35 m" agrees with Att D 3.3.6 and the FAA WAAS Performance Standard’s LPV-200 VAL.

claim: Departure shares the row of initial, intermediate and non-precision approach in Annex 10 Table 3.7.2.4-1 (220 m accuracy, 10 s to alert). The EGNOS service definition’s summary of that table gives the row, departure included, a horizontal alert limit of 556 m (0.3 NM), the value the page applies. The PBN Manual uses 1 NM for the RNAV 1 and RNP 1 specifications used for departures, and the departure-mode value of the avionics is set by RTCA DO-229 (to confirm).
value: 555.6, 10 m (the HAL the page applies on departure, the NPA value), s
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Chapter 3 Table 3.7.2.4-1 and Note 2; EUSPA SoL SDD §6.2 Table 7; ICAO Doc 9613 Vol II Part B Ch. 3 §3.2.1.6; Part C Ch. 3 §3.2.1.2; RTCA DO-229
note: EGNOS SoL SDD v3.6 Table 7 (p. 23), which summarises Annex 10, lists HAL 556 m (0.3 NM) and 10 s for "Initial approach, Intermediate approach, NPA, Departure". An earlier reading of Annex 10 found no departure HAL in Note 2 of the table itself; a reviewer with Annex 10 and DO-229 should settle the departure-mode value (the earlier build used the terminal 1 NM).

claim: SBAS LNAV/VNAV alert limits: HAL 556 m, VAL 50 m.
sources: RTCA DO-229; FAA Global Positioning System Wide Area Augmentation System (…; ICAO Doc 9613 Vol II, RNP APCH, 5.3.3.3.1.2 a) Note
ai_rationale: The FAA WAAS Performance Standard (through ESA Navipedia, read) gives LNAV/VNAV HAL 556 m and VAL 50 m, matching the code. Doc 9613 (read) confirms SBAS vertical guidance may serve LNAV/VNAV minima, and Doc 9849 Table 2-1 Note 3 that these are not Annex 10 table values. DO-229 was not read, so a reviewer with it should tick the claim.

claim: The time to alert is the longest time allowed from a fault to the alert in the cockpit.
ai_rationale: Annex 10 Ch. 3 definitions and Doc 9849 (3rd ed.) §2.2.2.3, both read, define the time to alert as the longest time from the system being out of tolerance to the alert in the aircraft; the plain wording matches. The cited 5th-edition section §2.2.4.4 was not checked.

claim: ADS-B broadcasts the GNSS position with an integrity indicator (NIC) taken from the receiver’s horizontal protection level; the ground system checks it against what the surveillance service needs, so the controller can trust the position on the screen.
note: NIC from the protection level is RTCA DO-260B / EUROCAE ED-102A practice, not read for this registry.
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §1.4.3 (read) supports ADS-B broadcasting the GNSS position. The integrity ADS-B carries (NIC) comes from the receiver’s horizontal protection level, not from the alert limits, and the ground system checks it against what the surveillance service needs; the text now says so. NIC from the protection level is DO-260B practice, from both reviewers’ expertise, not read.

claim: States verify SBAS performance and issue NOTAMs for degradations, using a service volume model.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.3.4.1; ICAO Annex 10 Attachment D 6.2.6
ai_rationale: Annex 10 Att D 6.2.6 (read) expects a State to provide status monitoring and a NOTAM system, using a service volume model, before publishing SBAS procedures, and Doc 9849 (3rd ed.) §7.11 (read) says the same. Annex 10 is now cited as the primary source; the 5th-edition section number was not checked.

claim: On loss of GNSS: inertial systems, DME (DME/DME updating), VOR/DME, ILS, radar (surveillance) and procedures by crews and ATC.
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §7.13.2.1 (read) lists on-board equipment such as IRS, conventional aids and radar, and procedural methods by aircrew and/or ATC, and names DME/DME updating, VOR/DME and ILS. The claim left out radar and used "procedural control", an ATC term the source does not use; it now follows the source.

claim: ICAO space weather advisories cover the ionosphere (total electron content and scintillation).
ai_rationale: ICAO space weather advisories (Annex 3, guidance in Doc 10100) cover HF COM, SATCOM, GNSS and radiation, and the GNSS advisory is driven by scintillation and vertical TEC; this is from expertise, as Annex 3 and Doc 10100 were not read. Doc 4444 §9.1.3.8 (read) requires ATS units to pass on space weather information affecting GNSS.

claim: With GPS alone (ABAS) the GNSS approach goes down to LNAV minima: GNSS gives no vertical protection level, so vertical guidance needs Baro-VNAV (LNAV/VNAV minima) or SBAS (LPV).
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §1.4.2.2; ICAO Doc 9849 §4.2
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §1.4.2.2 (read) says ABAS supports RNP APCH to LNAV minima and, with Baro-VNAV, to LNAV/VNAV minima. As written, the claim implied that aircraft with GPS alone never fly vertically guided approaches; it now says vertical guidance needs Baro-VNAV or SBAS. "No vertical protection level" is right for GNSS alone.

claim: Radiotelephony for GNSS problems, as PANS-ATM (Doc 4444 §12.3.1.14–12.3.1.15) gives it: a controller warns "GNSS REPORTED UNRELIABLE (or GNSS MAY NOT BE AVAILABLE [DUE TO INTERFERENCE]) IN THE VICINITY OF (location) (radius)" or "SBAS UNAVAILABLE FOR (specify operation)"; a crew whose navigation performance has degraded reports "UNABLE RNP (specify type) [DUE TO (reason)]".
note: Checked against the 16th edition incl. Amendment 8; "SBAS UNAVAILABLE FOR (specify operation)" shortens "BASIC GNSS (or SBAS, or GBAS) UNAVAILABLE FOR (specify operation) [FROM (time) TO (time) (or UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE)]". Later amendments to confirm.
ai_rationale: Read in Doc 4444 (16th ed. incl. Amendment 8) §12.3.1.14–12.3.1.15: the controller phrases, the SBAS phrase "SBAS UNAVAILABLE FOR (specify operation)" and the crew’s "UNABLE RNP (specify type) [DUE TO (reason)]". The claim had been written from memory; it now quotes the paragraphs with their sections. ICAO APAC guidance of August 2026 (read) quotes the same words; later amendments are still to confirm.

claim: The ionospheric delay follows the sun (time of day, season, 11-year cycle); storms make it change fast and unevenly over wide areas.
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §5.5.1–5.5.2 (3rd ed., read) ties the delay to time of day, season and the 11-year cycle, and says rare storms cause large, rapid variations over a wide area. "Thicker" was only half true, since storms can lower the electron content as well as raise it; the text now says the delay changes fast and unevenly, and the storm failure texts follow it.

claim: Near the magnetic equator, dense bands about 15° either side and post-sunset bubbles make single-frequency SBAS vertical guidance (APV, Category I) impractical.
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 (3rd ed., read) §5.5.5 describes dense bands about 15° either side of the magnetic equator and post-sunset bubbles, and says single-frequency SBAS APV is not practical there; Category I follows a fortiori. GAGAN’s APV-I certification shows that "impractical" means "not with high availability".

claim: Severe scintillation is common near the equator after sunset; it is patchy, takes out a few satellites at a time and affects every frequency.
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §5.5.3–5.5.4 (3rd ed., read): severe scintillation is fairly common near the equator after sunset and before midnight, occurs in patches, affects only a few satellites at a time and affects all GNSS frequencies. The claim matches point by point.

claim: The dual-frequency ionosphere-free combination removes the (first-order) ionospheric delay but amplifies noise and multipath by about 2.6.
ai_rationale: The ionosphere-free combination removes the first-order delay (Annex 10 Ch. 3 definition, read). With equal, independent noise on L1 and L5 the noise factor is √(γ² + 1)/(γ − 1) with γ = (f1/f5)² = 1.7933, i.e. 2.588, which the code computes exactly. The value rests on that derivation, since the 3rd edition of Doc 9849 does not give it.

claim: The GPS broadcast ionospheric model removes about half of the delay; SBAS reduces the error to a few metres and bounds it.
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §5.5.6 (3rd ed., read): the broadcast model reduces the ionospheric error by a factor of about two, and SBAS reduces it to a few metres with assured integrity. "Removes about half" and "bounds it" are faithful plain-language versions.

claim: The sizes of the ionospheric threat terms (the daytime band margin, the post-sunset threat, the storm) are illustrative, chosen to reproduce Doc 9849’s conclusions qualitatively.
ai_rationale: The threat sizes in iono.ts are labelled illustrative and tuned to reproduce Doc 9849’s qualitative conclusion (§5.5.5, read: single-frequency APV is not practical near the equator). No standard specifies them, and real GIVE threat models are system-specific and not public in this form, so this is acceptable for teaching.

claim: The magnetic (dip) equator is taken from IGRF (epoch 2025) every 15° of longitude (about 7°N over Indonesia).
sources: IAGA IGRF-14 inclination zero at ground level, epoch 2025.0; ICAO Doc 9849 §5.2.1.5
note: The earlier table, read from maps, put the line 2.5–3.3° too far north over Indonesia. At the 350 km shell height the line differs by at most 0.25° over 90–140°E.
ai_rationale: Both reviewers computed the dip equator (inclination zero) from IGRF-14 at epoch 2025.0 independently and got the same table: over Indonesia it lies at about 6.5–8°N, not 9–10°N, so the map-read table was 2.5–3.3° too far north at 90–120°E. The code now uses the IGRF-14 table, which moves Indonesia’s equatorial bands south (the recorded AirNav Indonesia values change, tests/golden). At the 350 km shell height the line moves by at most 0.25° over 90–140°E.

claim: Dual-frequency multi-constellation (DFMC) SBAS services for aviation are planned, not yet operational: the FAA plans WAAS dual-frequency service in stages from about 2026 (limited) to about 2028 (final); EUSPA’s 2026 roadmap places the EGNOS v3 DFMC service (release V3.2) in the early 2030s.
sources: FAA FAA Navigation Programs (D. Lawrence, CGSIC briefing) WAAS Phase 4 Dual Frequency Operations status; EUSPA EGNOS (programme status and roadmaps, EUSPA Industry Days… EGNOS infrastructure and services roadmaps; ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.4.5
ai_rationale: No DFMC SBAS safety-of-life service is operational. The FAA’s April 2026 CGSIC briefing (read) gives WAAS dual-frequency LOC about 2026, IOC about 2027 and FOC about 2028, and EUSPA’s 2026 roadmap (read) puts the EGNOS v3 DFMC service (V3.2) in the early 2030s; "EGNOS from 2028" had dated DFMC to the L1-only V3.1 release. The second reviewer preferred the 2026 EUSPA roadmap to EUSPA’s 2024 "about 2029", so this claim and egnos.v3-dfmc agree.

claim: Dual-frequency SBAS is expected to make approaches with vertical guidance possible, with high availability, in equatorial States.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §6.8.2
ai_rationale: Doc 9849 §6.2.5 (3rd ed., read) says future DFMC SBAS would be able to support nearly 100 % APV availability even in equatorial regions, and §5.5.3 that scintillation still affects all frequencies. The claim stated it as present fact for a service not yet in operation; it is now an expectation.

claim: ESSP (European Satellite Services Provider) is the EGNOS service provider for the Open Service and the Safety-of-Life service, under an up-to-ten-year contract with EUSPA signed in July 2022; EUSPA said in 2022 that it was taking over provision of the EGNOS Data Access Service (EDAS).
sources: EUSPA EGNOS Programme Status (EGNOS Workshop 2022) slide "New EGNOS Service Provision Phase"; EUSPA EUSPA taps ESSP for EGNOS service provider role; EUSPA SoL SDD §3.4.1
ai_rationale: ESSP is the EGNOS service provider for the Open Service and the SoL service (SoL SDD §3.4.1, read). EUSPA’s EGNOS Workshop 2022 slide (read by the second reviewer) records a contract of up to ten years signed with ESSP in July 2022, so the date stands, but EUSPA described the EDAS hand-over as in progress in 2022, so "took over" became "said it was taking over".

claim: EGNOS broadcasts its Safety-of-Life signal from GEO-1, SES-5 at 5°E (PRN 136), and GEO-3, Eutelsat 5 West B at 5°W (PRN 121, operational since 25 August 2025). GEO-2, ASTRA 5B at 23.5°E (PRN 123), moved to test on 5 September 2025.
sources: EUSPA EGNOS system release: GEO-3 satellite enters operational …; ESSP / EGNOS user support EGNOS Service Notice 33 Table 1; EUSPA SoL SDD §3.3.1 Table 2; EGNOS user support EGNOS user support, Realtime (GEO status); gps.gov GPS L1 C/A PRN code assignments
note: The gps.gov PRN list (January 2026) still gives ASTRA 5B at 31.5°E, its slot before 2023; the operator’s documents give 23.5°E.
ai_rationale: Service Notice 33 Table 1 and SoL SDD v3.6 Table 2 (both read) give GEO-1 SES-5 (PRN 136, 5°E) and GEO-3 Eutelsat 5 West B (PRN 121, 5°W) operational, and GEO-2 ASTRA 5B (PRN 123) in test since 5 September 2025, at 23.5°E. The claim’s 31.5°E came from the gps.gov PRN list, which still shows the slot ASTRA 5B left in 2023; the text and the geos.ts comment now say 23.5°E.

claim: Which EGNOS GEO is operational changes by service notice; the status shown is that of the September 2025 notices (Service Notices 33 and 34), still current on 5 October 2026 (EGNOS user support, Realtime).
sources: EGNOS user support EGNOS user support, Realtime (GEO status); ESSP / EGNOS user support EGNOS Service Notice 33; ESSP / EGNOS user support EGNOS Service Notice 34; ESSP / EGNOS user support EGNOS Service Notice 35
note: Check again just before an ESSP presentation.
ai_rationale: The EGNOS Realtime page, read on 5 October 2026, shows PRN 121 and 136 operational and PRN 123 in test, the configuration of Service Notices 33 and 34; Service Notice 35 (October 2025) reports an outage with full recovery and no GEO change. The text now carries the date; check it again just before a presentation.

claim: The EGNOS ground segment: 38 Ranging and Integrity Monitoring Stations (RIMS), two Mission Control Centres (MCC), two Navigation Land Earth Stations (NLES) for each GEO that uplink to the GEOs, and the EGNOS Wide Area Network (EWAN) (SoL SDD v3.6 §3.3.2).
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §3.3.2, §3.3.2.1, Figure 3
ai_rationale: SoL SDD v3.6 §3.3.2 (read) lists the RIMS network, two MCCs, two NLES for each GEO and the EWAN, and §3.3.2.1 says the current network has 38 RIMS (38 sites in Figure 3, counted by the second reviewer). "About 40" became 38, and the ESA page, which describes the pre-2011 architecture, is no longer cited.

claim: The two EGNOS mission control centres are at Torrejón (Spain) and Ciampino (Italy).
sources: European Commission 2017/1406 Annex; EUSPA SoL SDD §3.3.2
ai_rationale: The Annex of Implementing Decision (EU) 2017/1406 (read on EUR-Lex) names the mission control centres at Ciampino (Italy) and Torrejón (Spain), and SoL SDD v3.6 §3.3.2 (read) confirms there are two. The ESA page describing four centres is the old architecture and is no longer cited; no later amending decision was found, though EUR-Lex was not searched exhaustively.

claim: The ground sites shown: RIMS at Toulouse, Paris, Lisbon, Madeira, the Azores, La Palma, Athens, Lappeenranta and Kuusamo (sites in the 38-station network of SoL SDD v3.6, Figure 3); NLES at Aussaguel, Betzdorf, Burum, Cagliari, Fucino, Rambouillet and Redu (EU Implementing Decision 2017/1406). Only some of the sites are shown, at city level.
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §3.3.2.1, Figure 3; European Commission 2017/1406 Annex; ESSP EWA for SoL aviation users (ESSP presentation) slide 2 (SDD v3.5: removal of the ALY and ABS RIMS); ESSP / EGNOS user support EGNOS Service Notice 34
note: Alexandria (removed with SDD v3.5) and Kourou (not in v3.6 Figure 3) are no longer shown; the Finnish site is Lappeenranta (LAP) in EGNOS documents, which the Finnish National Land Survey calls Virolahti. Kuusamo is already in the 2017 decision. The NLES list was not re-checked against a later decision (Service Notice 34 confirms new NLES units at Rambouillet and Cagliari). Which NLES feeds which GEO is not stated in these sources; the page draws an example pairing and says so.
ai_rationale: SoL SDD v3.6 Figure 3 (read) has Toulouse, Paris, Lisbon, Madeira, the Azores, La Palma, Athens, Kuusamo and Lappeenranta, but not Alexandria (removed with SDD v3.5, per ESSP’s 2024 EWA slides) or Kourou, and no Virolahti label: EGNOS documents call the Finnish site Lappeenranta. The scenario now shows those nine RIMS, so its modelled network shrinks from 11 stations to 9. The NLES list matches the 2017 decision, and Service Notice 34 confirms new NLES units at Rambouillet and Cagliari. Re-checked on 7 October 2026 after the value changed: Figure 3 (PDF p. 20) labels Lisbon LSB, the Azores ACR and La Palma LPI (the scenario had LIS, AZO and SPC); the nine codes now match the figure and the service-area map.

claim: EGNOS RIMS span Europe and beyond, from the Canary Islands, Madeira and the Azores to Svalbard, Iceland and northern Finland, with stations also in North and West Africa, Turkey, the eastern Mediterranean, South Africa and Canada (SoL SDD v3.6, Figure 3).
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §3.3.2.1, Figure 3; European Commission 2017/1406 Annex
note: Service Notice 29 (October 2023) reported the Haifa RIMS temporarily out of operation; v3.6 Figure 3 still draws it. Drop "the eastern Mediterranean" if ESSP says it is out.
ai_rationale: Figure 3 of SoL SDD v3.6 (read) shows RIMS from the Canary Islands, Madeira and the Azores to Svalbard, Jan Mayen, Iceland and northern Finland, plus Agadir, Djerba, Nouakchott, Gölbaşı, Haifa, Hartebeesthoek and Moncton. Egypt and French Guiana are no longer in the network; the text now names the regions of Figure 3 (Nouakchott is West Africa). Haifa’s status should be confirmed with ESSP (Service Notice 29).

claim: Navigation land earth stations (NLES) uplink the EGNOS messages to the GEOs; each GEO has a primary and a backup uplink.
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §3.3.2.3; European Commission 2017/1406 Annex
ai_rationale: SoL SDD v3.6 §3.3.2.3 (read): the NLES are two for each GEO, one active and one back-up, and transmit the messages to the GEOs; the 2017 decision (read) lists the sites. The SDD replaces the old ESA page as the primary reference.

claim: The EGNOS Safety-of-Life service supports approaches with vertical guidance down to LPV-200 minima.
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §3.2.1
ai_rationale: SoL SDD v3.6 §3.2.1 (read): LPV-200 was declared with SDD v3.0 in September 2015, supporting RNP APCH down to LPV minima as low as 200 ft (Category I, VAL 35 m).

claim: The EGNOS Safety-of-Life service is open and free of direct charge to users.
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §1
note: Operational use still needs authorisation and, for an ANSP, an EGNOS Working Agreement (§3.4.3).
ai_rationale: SoL SDD v3.6 §1 (read) says the SoL service is provided openly and is freely accessible without any direct charge. Operational use still needs authorisation and, for an ANSP, an EWA (§3.4.3), which the note now says so that "free" is not read as "no agreement needed".

claim: EGNOS v2, in service, augments GPS on L1 only. EGNOS v3 is planned to add a dual-frequency multi-constellation (DFMC) service augmenting GPS and Galileo on L1 and L5; EUSPA’s 2026 roadmap places it in the early 2030s, after GPS L5 reaches full operational capability.
sources: EUSPA EGNOS (programme status and roadmaps, EUSPA Industry Days… EGNOS infrastructure and services roadmaps; EUSPA SoL SDD §1; §4.1.1 note 14
note: The roadmap gives no exact year; ask ESSP or EUSPA for the official V3.2 DFMC service date.
ai_rationale: SoL SDD v3.6 §1 (read) confirms that EGNOS today augments GPS L1 C/A and will augment GPS and Galileo on L1 and L5. The EUSPA Industry Days 2026 roadmaps (read, as images) start EGNOS v3 operations just after 2030 and place the DFMC service after GPS L5 full operational capability, so "around 2028" was out of date; the text says "early 2030s", the precision a bar chart allows.

claim: In the FAS data block, SBAS service provider 1 is EGNOS (0 WAAS, 2 MSAS, 3 GAGAN, 4 SDCM, 5 BDSBAS, 6 KASS, 7 A-SBAS; 15 any SBAS).
sources: EUROCONTROL SBAS FAS Data Block Tool, source reference documentation; ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B, SBAS provider IDs
ai_rationale: The EUROCONTROL FAS Data Block Tool (read) lists the provider IDs 0 WAAS, 1 EGNOS, 2 MSAS, 3 GAGAN, 4 SDCM, 5 BDSBAS, 6 KASS, 7 A-SBAS, 8–13 spare, 14 GBAS only and 15 any SBAS, citing DO-229D Appendix D and Annex 10 App B; the code’s 1 matches.

claim: ESSP’s NOTAM proposal service predicts when an EGNOS service level will be unavailable at airports with EGNOS-based procedures, formats the results as proposed NOTAMs (ICAO format, European Concept for GNSS NOTAM) and sends them by AFTN to the national NOTAM offices concerned, which validate and publish them.
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §3.4.4; ESSP EGNOS Service Provision Yearly Report
note: The page proposes NOTAMs for APV-I only, a simplification; whether ESSP proposes separate NOTAMs for LPV-200 is for ESSP to confirm.
ai_rationale: SoL SDD v3.6 §3.4.4 (read) describes the service: ESSP predicts service-level outages at given locations, formats NOTAM proposals in ICAO format following the European Concept for GNSS NOTAM, and sends them by AFTN to the NOTAM offices, which validate and publish them. The SDD does not limit it to APV-I, so the text now says "an EGNOS service level"; the page’s APV-I-only proposals are labelled a simplification.

claim: The proposed NOTAM the page writes uses the ICAO NOTAM items A (location), B and C (validity, UTC) and E (text); the wording of item E is illustrative, the Q line is left out, and the flight has no calendar date.
sources: EUSPA SoL SDD §3.4.4; ESSP EGNOS Service Provision Yearly Report
ai_rationale: The SDD (§3.4.4, read) confirms that proposals use an ICAO format following the European Concept for GNSS NOTAM, and items A, B, C and E are the right ICAO items. The page says the item E wording is illustrative and the Q line and calendar date are left out, so learners will not take it for a real ESSP proposal.

claim: The page forecasts LPV availability by running its own SBAS model forward at the airport with the conditions known in advance (a storm forecast, a planned RIMS outage); sudden failures such as a lost GEO are not in a forecast.
sources: ICAO Doc 9849 §4.3.3.4.1; EUSPA SoL SDD §3.4.4; ESSP EGNOS Service Provision Yearly Report
note: A real prediction uses the almanac, planned outages and the service volume model.
ai_rationale: The page forecasts with its own SBAS model and says that a real prediction uses the almanac, planned outages and the service volume model. Its split matches SDD §3.4.4 (read): scheduled events are notified at least 72 h ahead and unscheduled ones within 2 h after they occur, not predicted. The service.ts comment that listed a lost GEO among the forecast conditions has been fixed.

claim: To publish EGNOS-based (LPV) procedures, an air navigation service provider must sign an EGNOS Working Agreement (EWA) with ESSP. In March 2024, 85 EWAs were in force (46 of them with ATC providers), and 954 EGNOS-based procedures served 523 airports.
value: 85, 46, 954, 523 EWAs, of them with ATC providers, procedures, airports (March 2024)
sources: ESSP EWA for SoL aviation users (ESSP presentation) EWA breakdown and procedures slides; EUSPA SoL SDD §3.4.3
note: The other EWAs are with AFIS providers (25), military ANSPs (5), air operators (7) and aerodrome operators (2). The figures are from March 2024; ask ESSP for current ones.
ai_rationale: ESSP’s March 2024 EWA presentation (read) gives 85 EWAs in force (ATC 46, AFIS 25, air operators 7, military 5, aerodromes 2) and 954 EGNOS-based procedures serving 523 airports, and SDD §3.4.3 (read) says an EWA is required between ESSP and the ANSP. "46 with ANSPs" became "46 with ATC providers", "first step" became "must sign", and the page now shows the 523 airports. The figures are two and a half years old; ESSP can give current ones.

claim: With real EGNOS messages (EMS files, for example from EDAS), the map takes the UDREIs of the fast-correction messages and the ionospheric grid from the broadcast. It does not yet apply the Message Type 28 covariance (δUDRE), the degradation terms of Message Types 7 and 10 or the long-term corrections, and it interpolates only full 5° cells, so it would show no vertical guidance where the grid is 10° apart (north of 60°N). The map shipped today uses modelled corrections.
sources: RTCA DO-229 Appendix A; ESA EGNOS Message Server (EMS) User Interface Document
ai_rationale: The text understates what the real-message mode leaves out. interpolateGrid only uses four-IGP 5°×5° cells, whereas Annex 10 App B 3.5.5.5.4 requires falling back to 5° triangles and 10° cells, and between N60° and N75° uses 5°-by-10° cells; with the real EGNOS IGP mask (10° longitude spacing north of 60°N) no pierce point there gets a correction, so no LPV would be shown over Iceland or northern Scandinavia, where EGNOS serves to 72°N. groundFromDecoder also ignores MT28 δUDRE, MT6 UDREI updates and MT25 long-term corrections, besides MT7/MT10 degradation. Corrected as advised.
